The renewal equation says that new infections today depend on recent infections, weighted by the generation interval $w_s$, the chance that $s$ days separate an infection from the one it causes:

$$
I_t \sim \text{Poisson}\left(R_t \sum_{s \geq 1} I_{t-s}\, w_s\right)
$$

This tutorial simulates an outbreak with a known $R_t$, then estimates it back with the approach of [Cori et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwt133), written out in base R so every step is visible. You'll need **ggplot2** for the plots.

## 1. Set up the generation interval

A gamma distribution with a mean of six days, cut at three weeks.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(1)

days <- 1:120
w <- dgamma(1:21, shape = 6, rate = 1)
w <- w / sum(w)

infectiousness <- function(inc, t) {
  s <- 1:min(t - 1, length(w))
  sum(inc[t - s] * w[s])
}
```

## 2. Simulate an outbreak

$R_t$ is 1.5 until day 50, when a control measure brings it down to 0.8.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Simulated daily incidence."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of simulated daily cases over 120 days. Cases rise from about 5 a day to a peak of around 130 just before day 50, then fall steadily to under 10 a day by day 120."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
rt_true <- ifelse(days < 50, 1.5, 0.8)

inc <- numeric(length(days))
inc[1:5] <- 5

for (t in 6:length(days)) {
  inc[t] <- rpois(1, rt_true[t] * infectiousness(inc, t))
}

ggplot(data.frame(day = days, cases = inc), aes(day, cases)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#9A6714", width = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "Cases") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

## 3. Estimate Rt over a sliding window

With a gamma prior on $R_t$ (shape $a$, scale $b$) and a window of $\tau$ days, the posterior is also gamma, with shape $a + \sum I_t$ and rate $1/b + \sum \Lambda_t$, where $\Lambda_t$ is the total infectiousness on day $t$.

```{r}
tau <- 7
a <- 1
b <- 5

lambda <- c(0, sapply(2:length(days), \(t) infectiousness(inc, t)))

est <- data.frame(day = 15:length(days))
est$shape <- sapply(est$day, \(t) a + sum(inc[(t - tau + 1):t]))
est$rate <- sapply(est$day, \(t) 1 / b + sum(lambda[(t - tau + 1):t]))
est$mean <- est$shape / est$rate
est$lo <- qgamma(0.025, est$shape, est$rate)
est$hi <- qgamma(0.975, est$shape, est$rate)
```

## 4. Compare with the truth

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Estimated Rt with a 95% credible interval. The dashed line is the true value."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of estimated Rt from day 15 to day 120, with a shaded 95% credible interval and the true Rt as a dashed step that drops from 1.5 to 0.8 at day 50. The estimate starts near 2, settles close to 1.5 by day 30, falls to about 0.8 within a week of day 50 and stays near 0.8, with the band widening as cases fall."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(est, aes(day)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#9A6714", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean), colour = "#9A6714", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_step(data = data.frame(day = days, rt = rt_true), aes(y = rt), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#1D2930") +
  labs(x = "Day", y = expression(R[t])) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

The estimate tracks the true $R_t$ and takes about a window's length to catch up after the drop on day 50.

## 5. Try it yourself

The same simulation and estimator, running in your browser. Change a setting and the outbreak is simulated again and $R_t$ re-estimated. The true $R_t$ is fixed at 1.5, dropping to 0.8 on day 50.

Things to try:

- **Assume the wrong generation interval.** Leave the true mean at 6 days and set the analyst's to 4. The estimate is pulled towards 1: roughly 1.3 instead of 1.5 while cases grow, and 0.86 instead of 0.8 after the drop. Assume 9 days and it is pushed away from 1 instead.
- **Add imported cases.** Set 10 a day, then switch on *Count imported cases as local*. The estimate runs high throughout and creeps back towards 1 after the drop, because imported cases look like local offspring.
- **Widen the window.** Go from 7 to 21 days. The band narrows, but the estimate takes about two weeks, rather than four days, to fall below 1 after the drop.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import { genInterval, simulate, cori, labelRange, tidyPlot } from "./explorers.js"
```

::: {.explorer .ex-rt}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof trueMean = labelRange(Inputs.range([2, 20], { value: 6, step: 1, label: "True generation interval (mean, days)" }))
viewof assumedMean = labelRange(Inputs.range([2, 20], { value: 6, step: 1, label: "Generation interval the analyst assumes (days)" }))
viewof tau = labelRange(Inputs.range([1, 28], { value: 7, step: 1, label: "Estimation window (days)" }))
viewof imports = labelRange(Inputs.range([0, 20], { value: 0, step: 1, label: "Imported cases a day" }))
viewof lump = Inputs.toggle({ label: "Count imported cases as local", value: false })
viewof seed = Inputs.button("New random outbreak", { value: 4, reduce: v => v + 1 })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
rtTrue = (t) => (t < 49 ? 1.5 : 0.8)
sim = simulate({ rt: rtTrue, w: genInterval(trueMean), rpois: d3.randomPoisson.source(d3.randomLcg(seed)), imported: imports })
cases = sim.local.map((v, i) => ({ day: i + 1, local: v, imported: sim.imp[i] }))
minCases = 11
est = cori({
  local: lump ? sim.local.map((v, i) => v + sim.imp[i]) : sim.local,
  imp: lump ? null : sim.imp,
  w: genInterval(assumedMean),
  tau
}).map(r => (r.cases < minCases ? { ...r, mean: NaN, lo: NaN, hi: NaN } : r))
fmt = (day) => {
  const r = est.find(d => d.day === day);
  return r && Number.isFinite(r.mean) ? r.mean.toFixed(2) : "too few cases";
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p class="explorer-key" aria-hidden="true"><span><i class="sw sw-main"></i>Local cases</span>${imports > 0 ? html`<span><i class="sw sw-imported"></i>Imported cases</span>` : ""}<span><i class="sw sw-rule"></i><span>Day 50, when R<sub>t</sub> drops</span></span></p>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tidyPlot(Plot.plot({
  width, height: 190, marginLeft: 44, marginBottom: 36,
  ariaLabel: "Simulated daily cases",
  ariaDescription: `Bar chart of simulated daily cases over 120 days, peaking at ${d3.max(sim.local)} local cases on day ${sim.local.indexOf(d3.max(sim.local)) + 1}${imports ? `, plus ${imports} imported cases a day` : ""}.`,
  x: { label: "Day", domain: [0.5, 120.5] },
  y: { label: "Cases", grid: true },
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(cases, { x1: d => d.day - 0.42, x2: d => d.day + 0.42, y: "local", fill: "currentColor", ariaDescription: "local cases" }),
    Plot.rectY(cases.filter(d => d.imported), { x1: d => d.day - 0.42, x2: d => d.day + 0.42, y1: "local", y2: d => d.local + d.imported, fill: "currentColor", ariaDescription: "imported cases" }),
    Plot.ruleX([49.5], { stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4,3", ariaDescription: "drop" }),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
}))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tidyPlot(Plot.plot({
  width, height: 230, marginLeft: 44, marginBottom: 36,
  ariaLabel: "Estimated Rt against the true value",
  ariaDescription: `Estimated Rt with a 95% credible interval from day ${est[0].day}. The true Rt, dashed, is 1.5 until day 50 and 0.8 after. Estimate on day 40: ${fmt(40)}; on day 110: ${fmt(110)}.`,
  x: { label: "Day", domain: [0.5, 120.5] },
  y: { label: "Rt", grid: true, domain: [0, 3] },
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([1], { stroke: "currentColor", ariaDescription: "reference" }),
    Plot.areaY(est, { x: "day", y1: "lo", y2: d => Math.min(d.hi, 3), fill: "currentColor", clip: true, ariaDescription: "estimate band" }),
    Plot.lineY(est, { x: "day", y: d => Math.min(d.mean, 3), stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2, clip: true, ariaDescription: "estimate" }),
    Plot.lineY(d3.range(1, 121).map(day => ({ day, rt: rtTrue(day - 1) })), { x: "day", y: "rt", curve: "step-after", stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "5,4", ariaDescription: "true Rt" })
  ]
}))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p class="explorer-readout" aria-live="polite">Estimate on day 40: <strong>${fmt(40)}</strong> (true 1.5). On day 110: <strong>${fmt(110)}</strong> (true 0.8).</p>`
```

:::

The line is left out wherever the window holds fewer than 11 cases, where the estimate reflects the prior more than the data. Your browser draws its own random numbers, so the outbreak differs from the one above, which R generated with `set.seed(1)`.

::: {.callout-note}
## For mosquito-borne viruses
The generation interval for dengue or chikungunya includes the time the virus spends developing inside the mosquito, so it is longer than for a respiratory virus and changes with temperature. Imported cases also need separating from local ones, or they inflate $R_t$. See the [chikungunya primer](chikungunya-primer.qmd).
:::
